In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Qadr

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾

The pronoun in "anzalnahu" (We sent it down) refers to the Qur'an, definitively.

Al-Alusi related the consensus (ijma') on this, and said something indicating that there is a weak view, not to be taken into account, that it refers to Jibril.

What he said about the weakness of this view is supported by the context, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr: 4].

The well-known view is that "the Spirit" here is Jibril, peace be upon him, so the pronoun in "anzalna" refers to something other than him. The third-person pronoun was used to magnify the status of the Qur'an and to indicate its exalted rank.

It may be said: the mention of the surah of al-Qadr before it hints at this in His saying, ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾, and then came ﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾, i.e., the Qur'an that is recited. The attached pronoun in "inna" and "na" in "inna anzalnahu" is used for the plural and for magnification, and similarly "nahnu". Both occur together in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We [nahnu] sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], and what is meant by them here is definitively magnification, since plurality of the divine is impossible, or else the meaning of plurality is intended.

He has stated it explicitly elsewhere, with a clear word, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book, consistent, oft-repeated﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], and what is meant by it is definitively the Qur'an. This shows that the intent of those pronouns is the magnification of Allah, exalted is He.

This meaning and the sense of exclusivity are also suggested by the fronting of the attached pronoun "inna", and this context is a context of magnifying and exclusivity for Allah, glorified is He. Similar is: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ [al-Kawthar: 1], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent Nuh﴾ [Nuh: 1], ﴿Indeed, We, it is We who give life and cause death﴾ [Qaf: 43]. And the sending down of the Qur'an is a great blessing.

(p-31) It has been shown that the blessing is magnified, and Allah, glorified is He, is magnified, in His saying: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses﴾ [Sad: 29]. He said "a Book which We sent down" with the pronoun of magnification, then described the Book as "blessed".

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had earlier explicitly stated that it is for magnification, when speaking on the verse of Sad: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed﴾.

The reality is that the pronouns relating to Allah, exalted is He, come in plural forms for magnification and in singular forms. Among the plural forms is what has preceded; among the singular forms is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making on the earth a successive authority﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am creating a human from clay﴾ [Sad: 71], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

It is noticed in the singular forms that they occur in contexts of magnification and majesty: the first in the context of creating man from clay, which none can do except Allah; and the second in the context that He knows what the angels do not know, which is only for Allah, glorified is He. So whether the pronoun comes in plural or singular form, all of them contain magnification of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, whether by their explicit wording and original usage or by the context in the discourse.

Then it was disputed concerning what was sent down on the Night of Decree: is it the whole or a part?

It was said — and it is the view of the majority — that it is only the beginning of that surah, i.e., the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Then the revelation descended successively after that, and between its first and last there were twenty years."

It was said: what was sent down on that night is the entire Qur'an all at once, and all of it to the lowest heaven; then it began to descend upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in installments according to events.

This latter is the view of the majority, as we have previously mentioned, and the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, chose it when speaking on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Al-Alusi related it and related the consensus on it.

Ibn Hajar in Fath al-Bari, and Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, have a view that combines the two latter views, (p-32) namely that there is no contradiction between the two views, and they can be combined: that it was sent down as a whole to the lowest heaven on the Night of Decree, and the beginning of its first part, "Read in the name of your Lord" [al-'Alaq: 1], began to descend on the Night of Decree.

Around this issue there has arisen debate and theological argument concerning the manner of the Qur'an's descent, and they brought into it the claim that the Qur'an is created, that Jibril took it from the Preserved Tablet, and that Allah did not speak it when it was sent down upon the Messenger ﷺ.

Shaykh Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, may Allah have mercy on him, was asked about this; his answer was written and published, and it was sufficient. In it he quoted the words of Ibn Taymiyyah, and made clear that Allah, exalted is He, spoke it at its revelation, and he refuted every doubt on this.

The reality is that there is no contradiction, as has been said before, between its being in the Preserved Tablet, its descent to the lowest heaven as a whole, and its descent upon the Messenger ﷺ in installments; because its being in the Preserved Tablet — the Tablet contains everything that exists and will exist until the Day of Resurrection, and among that is the Qur'an which Allah will send down upon Muhammad ﷺ.

Its descent as a whole to the lowest heaven is like transferring a part of what is in the Tablet, which is the whole Qur'an; so the Qur'an came to exist in both the Preserved Tablet, like other things in it, and in the lowest heaven, and then it descends upon the Messenger ﷺ in installments.

It is known that it is also now present in the Preserved Tablet; the Tablet has not been empty of it. It may be argued for its descent as a whole and then its sending down in installments by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]; because "nazzala" with the doubled letter indicates repetition, like His saying: ﴿The angels descend﴾ [al-Qadr: 4], i.e., on every Night of Decree.

And "anzalnahu" has come, which indicates the whole.

The Sunnah has clarified the detail of its being sent down in installments upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and others, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When Allah decrees a matter in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon smooth rock, which penetrates them; until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say: 'What has your Lord said?' They say: 'The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'" The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari.

(p-33) And in Abu Dawud and others: "When Allah speaks with the revelation, the people of the heavens hear a sound like the dragging of a chain over smooth rock."

On this basis, the Qur'an exists in the Preserved Tablet when the Pen wrote what is and what will be; then it was transferred to the lowest heaven as a whole on the Night of Decree; then it descended in installments over twenty years. Whenever Allah wishes to send down a part of it, He, glorified is He, speaks what He wishes to send down, and Jibril, peace be upon him, hears it from Allah, exalted is He. There is no contradiction between these three states. And Allah knows best.

We have previously discussed the forms of the manner of revelation's descent and the Messenger's ﷺ reception of revelation.

It was said: the meaning of ﴿We sent it down on the Night of Decree﴾ is: We sent down the Qur'an concerning the status of the Night of Decree, magnifying it; so on this view it is not a time-frame.

The reality is that this view, although possible in terms of style, is made unnecessary by what follows it; because the magnification of the Night of Decree and the statement of its rank is that a Qur'an actually descended in it, and this is what immediately follows in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is? The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾ [al-Qadr: 2–3], to the end of the surah.

On this basis, the beginning of the surah concerns the sending down of the Qur'an and the statement of its time of descent, and the end of the surah concerns the Night of Decree and the statement of its rank.

The Night of Decree is mentioned in an unspecified way, but the Qur'an indicates the month in which it is, which is the month of Ramadan, by His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had earlier explained this in the surah of al-Dukhan: that it is the night in which every wise matter is decreed, and it is not the night of the middle of Sha'ban as some people claim.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had earlier explained the wisdom of its being sent down in installments, when speaking on His saying: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses, and that those of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Sad: 29].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-459) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Qadr

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾

There is no contradiction between this and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾ [al-Dukhan: 3], because the blessed night is the Night of Decree, and it is in Ramadan by the explicit text of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. So what many scholars claim, that the blessed night is the night of the middle of Sha'ban, is refuted by these Qur'anic texts.

And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 97, verse 3:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾

Al-qadr means elevation (rifah), and al-qadr can also mean measure (al-miqdar).

(p-34) Our shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, said in his memorandum of dictation (Mudhakkirat al-Imla') that there are two aspects to the reason it is named the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr):

The first: the meaning of qadr is nobility and elevated rank, as the Arabs say: "So-and-so is dhu qadr," meaning of elevation and honour.

The second aspect: it is named Laylat al-Qadr because Allah, exalted is He, decrees within it the events of the year. What supports this latter interpretation is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night. Indeed, We were ever warning.﴾ ﴿Therein is made distinct every precise matter.﴾ ﴿By command from Us.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 3–5].

Our shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, also mentioned this meaning in Surat al-Dukhan in Adwa' al-Bayan.

In fact, the surah contains what points to the first aspect, which is qadr as elevation and rank, namely His saying: ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾

So posing the question in this manner is for the sake of magnifying it, like His saying: ﴿The Striking Calamity.﴾ ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 1–3], and His saying: ﴿better than a thousand months﴾. In it there is explicit textual evidence of the loftiness of its rank and elevation, since in terms of time it equals more than eighty-three years, that is, more than the average lifespan of this nation.

Also, that it is singled out for the revelation of the Qur'an within it, and for the descent of the angels and the Spirit within it, and that it is peace until the rising of dawn, is sufficient proof of what is not shared by any other night of the year.

Accordingly, there is no objection to it being named Laylat al-Qadr, because it is the place where affairs are decreed each year, and by this and other things its rank is exalted and its status magnified. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

A reminder of a great blessing: if the deeds of the servant are multiplied on that night, so that it is better than a thousand months, as in this noble text, then when the servant happens to be in the Prophet's Mosque (al-Masjid al-Nabawi) praying, and a prayer there is worth a thousand prayers, how great will be the blessing and the magnitude of the favour from the Bestower, the Bountiful, glory be to Him. Indeed, this is among the things that raise aspiration and magnify desire.

I have limited the mention to the Prophet's Mosque rather than the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), with the greater multiplication (p-35) in it, because some exegetes said that the sin is multiplied in it as well.

Likewise, that is, the disobedience on the Night of Decree is like disobedience over a thousand months, and in the Sacred Mosque the servant is held to account for mere intention, so the danger is greater; while in Madinah there is safety.

Perhaps what supports this is that all the Nights of Decree were for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Madinah, and Ahl al-Sunnah have all affirmed this, whereas the Shi'ah claimed that it was abrogated and entirely lifted. This is not to be considered, because of the soundness of the near-mutawatir texts.

* *

A note

No specific determination has been given as to which Ramadan that night falls in, and the scholars have said much on this matter and cited texts.

Among the views, the most general is that it is in the whole year, which is what Ibn Mas'ud reported, and this brings nothing new; he only meant striving (al-ijtihad).

Another: that it is in the whole of Ramadan, which is according to the general wording of the Qur'an.

Another: that it is in the last ten nights of it, which is more specific than the previous.

Another: that it is in the odd nights of the last ten, which is more specific than the previous.

Another: that it is in the individual odd nights of the last ten.

It was said: on the twenty-first; it was said: the twenty-third; it was said: the twenty-fifth; it was said: the twenty-seventh; it was said: the twenty-ninth; and it was said: the last night of Ramadan specifically. Each of these has texts supporting it.

However, the most famous, most widespread, and soundest of them is what came that it is on the twenty-seventh and the twenty-first, and there is no need to recite the texts relating to each of these, for no book of tafsir has been left without mentioning them, especially Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi.

* *

A note

If all the texts that came concerning the odd nights of the last ten are sound, then it is not far-fetched that the Night of Decree revolves among them, and is not necessarily fixed on one of them nor outside them. It may fall in one year on the night of the twenty-first, while in another year it is the night of the twenty-fifth or the twenty-seventh, and in another the night of the twenty-third or the twenty-ninth, and so on. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

Ibn Kathir related this view from Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and others, and said: "It is the most likely," and Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

It has also been said: he ﷺ was made to forget it, so that the nation would strive throughout the whole month or throughout all ten nights. What confirms that it is in the last ten is that he ﷺ performed i'tikaf seeking the Night of Decree.

As for its virtues, what has been widely reported in the books of hadith and tafsir has come, and the noble text of the Qur'an suffices concerning it.

There are many discussions about this night, too lengthy to trace, among them what is mentioned of its signs.

Among them: some people's attempts to extract it from the Qur'an.

Among them: its connection to the rule of the Banu Umayyah. None of these has a text on which reliance can be placed, so there is no need to mention them, except what came in some signs of its day, the morning after it, where mention was made of something in the hadith: "And I saw myself prostrating on its morning in water and mud."

They mentioned among the signs of its day that the sun rises white, and they said: because the lights of the angels, when they ascend, meet the rays of the sun and produce in it a whiteness of light. This is related from Ubayy in Sahih Muslim.

Among them: the moderation of its air, its weather, and the like. Among what may have a connection to the surah itself is what Ibn Kathir related: that some of the early generation (al-salaf) sought to extract it from the Book of Allah within the surah itself, and said: the word "hiya" in His saying ﴿Peace it is﴾ [al-Qadr: 5] falls as the twenty-seventh word in counting its words, so it is the night of the twenty-seventh.

It was also said: the letters of the phrase Laylat al-Qadr are nine letters, and they are repeated three times, so their total is twenty-seven letters, so it is the night of the twenty-seventh.

Perhaps the most correct thing to say is what we have already put forward: that it falls within the odd nights of the last ten and does not go outside them. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

**The Exalted's words: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾.**

It has been said: "The Spirit" is Gabriel, as in His words: ﴿So We breathed into it of Our Spirit﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91]. "Therein" would then mean among the company of the angels. Or it is coordinated with "the angels," being a specific item joined to a general one (ʿatf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm).

It has also been said: the Spirit is a distinct kind of angel of its own, and "therein" is an adverbial complement of the descent, meaning in that night.

* *

The Exalted's words: ﴿from every matter﴾.

The word *amr* may be the singular of *umūr* (matters) and also the singular of *awāmir* (commands). What appears to be correct is that it includes both meanings together, because a matter (*amr*) among the matters only occurs through a command (*amr*) among the commands: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 82].

What supports this is what came about it in Surat al-Dukhān: ﴿Therein every wise matter is made distinct﴾ ﴿a command from Us﴾ [al-Dukhān: 4–5].

What is made distinct of the matter is one of the matters, since good and evil, harm and benefit, and so on, are separated in it. Then He said: ﴿a command from Us﴾, as the context indicates: ﴿There is no deity but He; He gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Dukhān: 8]. So every matter among the matters requires a command among the commands. This may be among the homonymous words (al-alfāẓ al-mushtarakah) used in both of their meanings. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 97, verse 5:

(p-38) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Peace it is until the emergence of dawn﴾.

It has been said: "Peace it is" means that the angels greet every believer they encounter.

It has also been said: "Peace it is" means that every matter in it is peace, and no one in it is afflicted with evil. In any case, there is no contradiction between the two views: the first is part of the second, because the second makes it (the night) a time for every good, and negates from it every evil. Among the great goods is the greeting of the angels upon the believers.

A subtle point:

That the descent of the Qur'an is mentioned here at night rather than in the day indicates the virtue of the night being singled out.

The Qur'an and the Sunnah have pointed to its counterparts. From the Qur'an is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra' 1], and among them His saying: ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory prayer for you﴾ [al-Isra' 79], ﴿And from the night, glorify Him, and after the prostrations﴾ [Qaf 40], ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night is firmer in impression and more upright in speech﴾ [al-Muzzammil 6]. And His saying: ﴿They used to sleep little of the night﴾ [al-Dhariyat 17].

From the Sunnah is his saying (ﷺ): "When the last third of the night remains, our Lord descends to the lowest heaven..." the hadith.

This indicates that the night is especially suited to divine breezes and to the manifestations of the Lord, glory be to Him, to His servants, because of the heart's emptiness, the cutting off of preoccupations, and the stillness of the night; and solitude is more effective in bringing the heart's presence and purity.
